abstract:
Breast cancer (BRCA) is one of the most prevalent malignancies in women. Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) and its receptor CD74 molecule (CD74) have been implicated in tumor immunity, yet their functional interplay within the BRCA microenvironment remains unclear.
Transcriptomic datasets and single-cell RNA sequencing analyses were performed to assess the expression patterns, prognostic significance, and cellular localization of MIF and CD74. Their functional interactions were further investigated using an in vitro co-culture system of MCF7 BRCA cells and macrophages, combined with MIF inhibition and CD74 blockade.
MIF and CD74 were significantly upregulated in BRCA and associated with poor prognosis. Single-cell analysis showed that CD74 was predominantly expressed in tumor-associated macrophages, whereas MIF was mainly produced by cancer cells. Tumor-derived MIF promoted M2 macrophage polarization through CD74-mediated activation of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT) signaling pathway, and this effect was abolished upon disruption of this signaling axis. Hypoxia was identified as a critical upstream regulator driving MIF secretion.
These findings identify a hypoxia-driven MIF/CD74 signaling axis that promotes immunosuppressive macrophage polarization in BRCA, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target.
